bodyOriginal.text: [Bucket Mouse] has long been a fan of the various iterations of the Nintendo Game Boy. Now, he’s turned his eye to the Game Boy Advance, building an enhanced version for the console’s 25th anniversary.

There are plenty of ways to mod an existing GBA to be better than the original, but this build recreates the console from the ground up. It’s basically a brand new motherboard that replaces the original entirely, requiring only the CPU and RAM to be harvested from the original board.

It’s perfect for when you find a badly-damaged handheld that needs heavy repair, because every other part on the board can be purchased new. You can buy a nice shiny screen kit online, and even upgrade to LiPo power if so desired. The new motherboard also eliminates sound issues that are common when upgrading the screen in a classic GBA, and there’s stereo audio available on the headphone jack as standard. Battery life is also improved compared to the original.

If you’ve got a haggard old GBA in need of repair, or you just want to build the best classic handheld you can, it’s worth taking a look at this build. You might also appreciate previous works from [Bucket Mouse], like his efforts to improve the original Game Boy.

bodyOriginal.text: Damage to nuclear DNA occurs constantly, and near all of it is immediately repaired. A tiny fraction lingers, however, and over time a burden of mutational damage builds up in tissues throughout the body. It is an open question as to how large a component of degenerative aging is a direct result of this damage, under normal circumstances. High rates of mutation in individuals with disabled DNA repair mechanisms shorten life span and accelerate the onset of age-related conditions, sometimes dramatically, but that doesn't necessarily mean the DNA damage is important in aging at levels exhibited in normal individuals. The best approach to firm data is to find a way to suppress or repair mutations without affecting other mechanisms, but the life-extending interventions that are known to slow the accumulation of DNA damage also have many other beneficial effects on metabolism. As reported here, for example, calorie restriction slows the pace at which the burden of DNA damage grows over time. Calorie restriction also improves cell function and health in numerous other ways, however, producing sweeping changes in the operation of cells and systems throughout the body that are unrelated to DNA damage.

Past studies in animals have shown that a large reduction in the number of calories they consume, called caloric restriction, extends their lifespans and slows aspects of aging. But whether caloric restriction also slows the rate at which mutations occur with age had not been investigated across the genome , the complete set of genetic material present in every cell. A new study has shown that caloric restriction reduced the level of mutations across several tissues in mice that were fed 30 percent fewer calories than they would have ingested if allowed to eat freely.

The study analyzed the effect of caloric restriction on different types of genetic changes. They found that to varying degrees across tissues, it dialed down the level of substitution mutations , in which one DNA letter is swapped for another, and insertion and deletion mutations, in which one or more DNA letters are added to or missing from the genome. The study results also showed that the impact of caloric restriction varies across tissues and cell types, as well as across the genome. For example, liver cells showed a greater reduction in mutation burdens with caloric restriction than kidney or brain cells.

Surprisingly, in liver and kidney cells, the reduction in the number of mutations from caloric restriction was greatest in the least-active regions of the genome, which contain either no genes or genes not being used by a given cell. One possible explanation is that if caloric restriction reduces DNA damage across the genome, active regions of the genome would not benefit as much because those regions already repair DNA damage frequently.

bodyOriginal.text: Artist Isamaya Ffrench has opened her second-ever Studio Iron show as part of this year's London Design Festival , with participants including Andu Masebo and Barnaby Lewis .
Studio Iron is the brainchild of Ffrench , a makeup artist and creative director, who launched her collectible design gallery at Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

bodyOriginal.alt: Studio Iron at LDF

bodyOriginal.text: Isamaya Ffrench has opened her second Studio Iron show The project is back for London Design Festival (LDF), on display as part of curator Alex Tieghi-Walker's Perfectly Imperfect programme in the Brompton Design District.
Ffrench selected 27 creatives for the exhibition, featuring pieces that challenge ideas about what materials go together.

bodyOriginal.alt: Cowhide armchair

bodyOriginal.text: Armchairs by Andu Masebo and Thomas Cardiff feature in the show "Our designers are based all over the world, and as someone who's highly into the tactility of objects and art, it was amazing to see all the pieces in real life," she told Dezeen. "To see how they looked, what they felt like, and to witness their scale."
"Most of the time, we get to experience art and design on the internet, in museums or in shops as the finished piece with great lighting and great props," she continued.

"But I'm more interested in the process, the tools, the raw materials, and the industrial machines. It's a real privilege to be in an artist's space and to talk to them about their inspiration or see them at work."

bodyOriginal.alt: Studio Iron by Isamayya Ffrench

bodyOriginal.text: Various contrasting materials make up the pieces Among the selection is a low-slung hammered steel pouf by Jesse Butterfield , topped with a lacy linen cushion by Jane Wright .
Opposite the pouf, an oversized, angular armchair by tattoo artist Thomas Cardiff is on display, crafted from a steel frame with a cowhide-clad seat and tattooed leather sides.

bodyOriginal.alt: Perfectly Imperfect

bodyOriginal.text: They form part of the Perfectly Imperfect exhibition in west London Marten Herma Anderson is showing a bloated resin lamp with a gridded pattern and a nickel-plated brass base, while Atelier Fomenta is presenting a bulb encased in a cylindrical slab of rubber held together with rivets.
A tangled stainless steel coat rack by Andu Masebo was placed in the corner of the gallery, close to a chunky hammered steel mirror, also by Butterfield.

bodyOriginal.alt: Silver ash tray

bodyOriginal.text: Different-sized furniture and objects make up the selection Blacksmith Barnaby Lewis 's spindly, skeletal chair features in the show, alongside a stainless steel floor lamp by Wretched Flowers , cloaked in chainmail, gemstones and glass beads.
Lewis is among the London-based rising talents spotlighted in the Dezeen Dispatch newspaper we published for LDF.
"Barnaby's practice is visceral and poetic at the same time and he's also wildly prolific," Ffrench told Dezeen. "His work deserves more attention."

Read: London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches London-based Ffrench said that she hopes to expand Studio Iron, which is still in its infancy, into an interdisciplinary creative agency that champions young designers.
"London feels genuinely open in terms of how people work," said the artist. "There's less pressure to attach yourself to a single practice, which makes it easier to move between disciplines."

bodyOriginal.alt: Studio Iron exhibition

bodyOriginal.text: Rubber and resin were used to create some of the show's lamps "Galleries and shops are also much more inclined to represent and sell the work of emerging artists versus established ones," added Ffrench. "And I think it is vital to support them and help them grow."

bodyOriginal.text: A Matti Suuronen Futuro House has been manufactured for the first time in decades and decked out by Finnish design brand Marimekko for Helsinki Design Week .
The famously flying-saucer-like structure recently landed in Kaisaniemi Botanical Gardens as part of the Finnish capital's annual design festival .
Initially conceived as a transportable ski cabin by Finnish architect Matti Suuronen in 1968, the Futuro House is among the most distinctive emblems of space-age architecture.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House at Helsinki Design Week 2026

bodyOriginal.text: The first new Futuro House for decades made an appearance at Helsinki Design Week. Photo by Justus Hirvi Prefrabricated in fibreglass-reinforced plastic, it was once described by British critic Justin McGuirk as "the closest housing ever came to product design".
Despite being intended for mass production, fewer than 100 were made worldwide. Manufacture ceased shortly after the 1973 oil crisis, which sent the price of plastic rocketing.
Around 60 are estimated to still be in existence, scattered across the globe in varying states of repair.

That number became one greater recently for the first time in decades, thanks to a project that began in 2024 when Dutch-American preservationist architect Jan van Dijs was alerted by a friend and client to an unusual post on Facebook.
An executive at a Finnish materials firm, Exel Composites, was selling the original Futuro moulds.
"How fascinating if we could actually do this"
At this point, Van Dijs, who has spent much of his career restoring mid-century houses in California , was only vaguely familiar with the Futuro Houses.
"I dug in a little bit, I started to learn about the history," he told Dezeen. "And I start to realise that it's something of a fascinating story."

"And I really had my doubts that all the pieces were there, that they could be restored, so I tried to keep all of that in check," he added. "But I certainly had started to make an emotional connection to how fascinating this could be if we could actually do this."
Twenty Futuro Houses had been fabricated in its native Finland originally, by plastics company PolyKem.

Exel had acquired PolyKem's assets, including the Futuro moulds, after the fabricator went bankrupt in the early 1990s – a difficult period for Suuronen that reportedly culminated in him and his wife losing their home.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro moulds

bodyOriginal.text: The moulds were in a sorry state when van Dijs first saw them. Photo by Jan van Dijs In the decades since production stopped, the moulds had been periodically moved between various forms of storage without a purpose.
Suuronen died in 2013, and so once hooked on the Futuro story, Van Dijs spent several months trying to engage with the architect's family.

"I couldn't just buy the moulds and build this thing – I needed to have a license, and I needed to have their support," he said. "The reality was, unless I could do that, there was no future for this project."
The Suuronens were hesitant, having been contacted several times over the years about poorly thought-through schemes on a similar theme.
But eventually they were persuaded with help from the Exel man, Jyrki Aho, who died a short while later.
When Van Dijs flew out to see the moulds in May 2025, they were languishing in a field and nearly 60 years old.
"The exterior of the moulds looked like hell," he remembered. "I mean, there was grass growing out of them and moss covering them, and it looked really bad."

Nevertheless, the decision was made to proceed, and Van Dijs worked with Finnish plastic fabrication company Ekin Muovi to restore the moulds and recast the panels with the aim of producing a faithful reconstruction of Suuronen's design.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House moulds

bodyOriginal.text: The pieces had been drifting into decay since the 1970s. Photo by Jan van Dijs Even the same paint colours were used, having been matched from scraps that remained on the moulds.
It was a step into the unknown for Van Dijs, and he admits the process was trickier than he had anticipated.

While today plastic moulding uses two tessellating pieces – one to pour the cast into and one to press over it to squeeze out all the air – Suuronen's are one-part moulds, meaning air bubbles must be eliminated manually.
"It's all hand labour," said Van Dijs. "Nobody does it like that anymore."
Casting a single panel therefore took days instead of hours and was very labour-intensive – "no doubt a large contributor to the problems faced by the Futuro in the 1970s", Van Dijs suggests.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House fabrication

bodyOriginal.text: Casting the new Futuro panels was a painstaking process. Photo by Jan van Dijs There were pleasant surprises as well, however. Unexpectedly, the moulds being sold by Exel included furniture designs by Suuronen, which have also been reproduced as part of the project.
They include built-in lounge chairs, a dining table, and the Orbit chair.

The fabrication process took five months, including some mishaps along the way. Including the restoration of the moulds, Van Dijs estimates the project has cost around 450,000 Euros, though he hopes further Futuros would cost less than 300,000.

In late June of this year, the 21st Futuro House to be made in its native country was completed, ready to be transported in several pieces for reassembly at its temporary home on the Kaisaniemi lawns.

bodyOriginal.alt: Half-built Futuro House

bodyOriginal.text: The new Futuro was manufactured in five months, completing in late June. Photo by Jan van Dijs For the Helsinki Design Week installation, Marimekko was invited to create an interior for the new Futuro House.
It opted to divide the open space into three areas – one for lounging and sleeping, one for eating and working, and a kitchenette.
"It was really important to sort of create a proposal for future ways of living," Marimekko creative director Rebekka Bay told Dezeen.

"That sounds like a big, grand statement, but we were really just intrigued by how we would live in the Futuro House today. I think there is a real trend for downscaling, and we felt that the Futuro House is sort of speaking to that."

bodyOriginal.alt: Marimekko installation at Helsinki Design Week 2026

bodyOriginal.text: Marimekko wanted its Futuro installation to feel "tactile, lived-in". Photo by Justus Hirvi Marimekko products were displayed on perspex shelving units that double as transparent room dividers, while stripy prints created for the brand during a residency by Danish textile artist Vibeke Rohland were used to upholster the furniture.
"It would have been obvious for us, of course, to go back to our archives and find prints that were designed in 1968 when the house was also designed," said Bay.

"But we wanted to take the opposite route and propose something that had been created today. We convey certain images when we speak to the future, but we wanted our proposal to be sort of tactile, lived-in, friendlier, and were therefore intrigued to use brand new textile designs."
With design week over, discussions about the structure's future are now ongoing, though Van Dijs said his preference is for it to remain on public display in Finland.

bodyOriginal.alt: Marimekko Futuro House installation

bodyOriginal.text: The brand's products were displayed on transparent shelving units. Photo by Justus Hirvi "I hope it will move somewhere into the countryside and someone will be using it as their summer cabin," said Bay. "I think that would be wonderful."
Van Dijs also plans to produce new Futuro Houses to order – but the run will be limited.
"Casting moulds are just like the plates for a print; they are designed for a limited number of editions," he said.
"I think the original moulds were probably near the end of their lifespan when production stopped. Through a significant effort we were able to extend their life, but not forever."

Read: "What if houses were designed like bikes?" He estimates that the restored moulds will support producing between four and six new Futuros. After that the moulds will be destroyed, and, in Van Dijs's words, "that will be the end of the original Futuros".
In his design, Suuronen focused on making the Futuro House quick to assemble, quick to heat and suitable for difficult terrains.
But it is also cramped, tricky to transport and dreadfully insulated, leaving it without an obvious practical use in 2026.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House at Helsinki Design Week

bodyOriginal.text: Plans for the Futuro's next home are still being finalised. Photo by Justus Hirvi Nevertheless, Van Dijs is adamant that Suuronen's creation is more than mere whimsy.
"I would love to leave my home every day and go to my Futuro office, a small apartment, yoga studio, architectural book store," he suggested.

He regards the Futuro as an important touchstone for radical post-war optimism and creativity – the same conditions from which Marimekko was born in 1951 – and sees his project as a reigniting of that spirit.
"I think the Futuro should be considered an icon of Finnish design, which was not the case when it was originally produced," he said.
"This project allows us to see the Futuro as Matti Suuronen envisioned it – I think that's important."

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: in a time of dopamine design and AI tools , a group of design industry professionals at an Arca talk discussed what role colour is playing in the contemporary American home.
Colours such as olive greens and a shade called Black Martini are in, according to Tony Piloseno, owner of Orlando-based company Tonester Paints .
Piloseno joined interior designers Kati Curtis and Tamara Feldman for a conversation at Mexican stone company Arca' s showroom in Miami, moderated by Dezeen US editor Ben Dreith.
And while the panellists agreed that rich, dark colours are in at the moment, the most important element of contemporary colour usage is about experience and reevaluating how people choose colour.

bodyOriginal.alt: Arca Wynwood

bodyOriginal.text: Arca and Dezeen hosted a talk at the Mexican stone company's Wynwood Miami showroom "I use tons of colour in my work, but what I'm thinking about, more so than trends, is how are we using colour?" said Curtis. "Are we using colour as an applied element, or is colour actually architecture?"
Both Curtis and Feldman referenced the work of Mexican modernist architect Luis Barragán in their framing of colour as more than a trendy accent.

"The term colour blocking has always bothered me because I feel like it's an accent – it's like putting wallpaper on one wall," continued Curtis. "It feels to me like you ran out of money, and you just went with that."

bodyOriginal.alt: Dezeen pane

bodyOriginal.text: The panellists included (from left) Ben Dreith, Tamara Feldman, Kati Curtis and Tony Piloseno An expanded conception of colour utilises light, texture, and the aim should be to envelop whoever is in a space. The panellists noted how the presence of tinted glass in Miami makes this even more important.
This, for Feldman, means that the whole of an interior – including light – and all the way through to the artwork on the walls should work together.
"I don't think it's just about a colour and a wall," she said. "I think it's the whole concept together."

Feldman is currently designing a coffee pavilion for the Institute of Contemporary Art in Miami, where she has used mirrors and Arca's Umbria-fabricate tiles to create a sculptural work in the institution's gardens.

bodyOriginal.alt: Tony Piloseno with microphone

bodyOriginal.text: Piloseno spoke on contemporary colour trends and specifying techniques The idea that colour should envelop and create an emotional response has become a hot topic recently, with the emerging trend of so-called "dopamine design" seeing spaces covered in bright colours and mish-mashed patterns to stimulate the mind.

The panellists agreed that colour can work to make you feel at ease, comfortable or inspired, but that this is more related to individual preference and experience than any set configuration or style.

"Does the room look really cool on TikTok, then you hate it 15 minutes later because you threw it in there to try to create this cool picture?" asked Curtis. "It can definitely go in the wrong direction too if you don't know what you're doing."

bodyOriginal.alt: Tamara Feldman

bodyOriginal.text: The panellists agreed on the usefulness of AI but highlighted the personal aspects of colour selection and design Piloseno added that dark colours that wash over you can have a positive effect as well.
"There is a direct emotional impact that colour has, especially with these darker colours," he said.

The panellists also addressed AI in design, and how choosing a colour scheme can be risky. For example, once you apply the paint or veneer, it takes a significant amount of work to pivot in a different direction.
Visualisation tools have existed for years, but Curtis said that generative AI has allowed her to show clients what a space might look like more easily before they commit.

"Even if it's not an accurate representation of exactly what the colour is going to be, I think it's very helpful in giving clients an idea of the overall room rather than just testing a sample," said Curtis.
"What AI and just any kind of colour visualiser tool will help with is seeing the specific colour vertically or how it's going to look on the ceiling with specific shadows," added Piloseno.
Ultimately, though, the panellists agreed that the pursuit of colour, and whatever downstream emotional effects, requires a human touch.
"I think the whole process of selecting colours is very personal," said Piloseno. "You shouldn't have AI guide you to these specific colours."

bodyOriginal.alt: Arca showroom Dezeen talk

bodyOriginal.text: The event brought out a large crowd of Miami professionals The speakers added that personal relationships and understanding the emotions of clients are paramount.
Colour choices often represent this dynamic more than other aspects of design. If a designer is going to understand what will engage the mind, they need to know the mind in question.
"What we do is really part therapy, part design," said Feldman.

Technology underwrites the process while the person guides the choices on the table. And while neuroscience has created new streams for engaging with design schemes, Curtis said that the foundations remain as important as ever.
"As long as you stick with those fundamental elements that we all know, we can mix all of those things in a really beautiful way," added Feldman. "That's going to make everybody's dopamine work."

bodyOriginal.text: A pasta-shaped daybed and speakers that resemble Saturn's rings are among the products on display at Contemporary Design Selections at this year's Lake Como Design Festival .

The eighth edition of the Contemporary Design Selections show, curated by Giovanna Massoni , follows the festival theme of Borders, encouraging participating designers, architects and makers to consider boundaries in design.
The theme could be interpreted through materiality, form, function or design's relation to other disciplines, while the open call also highlighted the social and political elements of the industry.
The exhibition is located at Villa Saporiti, which marks the first public showcase in the neoclassical building, and displays 57 projects by designers and studios from 30 countries.
The showcase features furniture, lighting, functional objects and textiles selected by Massoni across 10 rooms in the villa and its outdoor spaces.
Read on for seven design pieces that caught our attention:

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of metal and leather chairs by Studio Bjorn Verlinde

bodyOriginal.text: Belgium-based Studio Bjorn Verlinde spotlighted its minimal Fur seating and side table collection at the exhibition.
Designed for restless people, the series features an unconventional backless rocking chair with a curved aluminium base that allows the user to gently lean back.
A contrasting seat made from brown leather sits atop the base of the chair, which is mirrored by the surface of the accompanying table.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of light by Massimo Rigaglia

bodyOriginal.text: Massimo Rigaglia , a Milan-based artist and designer, created the Lights in Tension light collection from strips of flexible bamboo held in place by leather cords.
The result is a lightweight, curved structure anchored by a brass base that "embraces fragility as an aesthetic value", said Rigaglia.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of travertine and glass tables

bodyOriginal.text: BR Collection by Studio Alessandra Hofmann
These coffee tables by Basel-based Studio Alessandra Hofmann were informed by brutalist architecture.
The cube-shaped blocks of travertine are intersected with rectangular slabs of handmade cast glass, creating two levels to the tabletop.
The designer took an experimental approach to working with natural materials, embracing reactions created in the design process such as bubbles in the glass and open pores in the travertine.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of speakers by ArmoniusLab

bodyOriginal.text: Founded by designer Elia Dusi, ArmoniusLab presented its Saturnia speakers, where the audio unit is encompassed by acid-treated iron that resembles Saturn's rings.

The speaker was designed to be placed on the floor and tilt upwards, so sound travels "not directly to the listener, but around the room," the studio explained, creating a different style of listening experience.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of day bed by Studio YellowDot

bodyOriginal.text: Studio YellowDot collaborated with pasta company Barilla's 3D-printed pasta project Artisia to create a daybed that resembles the food's shape.
The hollow furniture, which was 3D printed in one piece from a wood fibre and bioplastic composition, features a ribbed surface similar to the pasta.
According to the studio, it responded to the festival's Borders theme by highlighting the border between food technology and design.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of 10-metre-long rug

bodyOriginal.text: This 10-metre-long wool rug by textile studio The Happy Few was designed to reflect the experience of walking down the street, with rectangular woven blocks resembling street tiles.
The designers sought to tell a story of seasonal changes through its colour palette, with shades of grey and blue transitioning to brown and green.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of room divider

bodyOriginal.text: Ceramics and furniture studio Whats Wrong Duo designed the Claustra room divider, which was informed by the soft lines and transparency found in the natural world.
Comprised of brown, purple, cream and grey hues, the furniture is made from aluminium and ceramic pieces, with the Bucharest- and Zurich-based studio also creating the glazes for the clay.
Through this design,the duo aimed to explore the boundary between a functional space divider and artistic expression.

bodyOriginal.text: A great deal of advocacy for the development of therapies to slow and reverse aging has moved on from a focus on reducing suffering. That the majority of the arguments now focus on economic productivity and reduced entitlement costs reflects a broad and possibly quite correct cynicism about what motivates the politicians, wealthy political influencers, and bureaucrats who collectively control the largest flows of funding and support in our societies. Private funding for research and development focused on longevity remains very motivated by the potential reduced suffering, and indeed the potential to reduce one's own personal suffering in the years ahead. However, the longevity industry of the recent past, and for the near future, exists in a state of tension as it attempts to make the transition from a privately supported new venture to an established field supported by the full panoply of state controlled medical systems - to be as openly and comprehensively backed by governments as cancer research and development.

Most advocates these days appear to believe that the way to make this happen is to exploit the high level of anxiety in the ruling classes of much of the world that centers around the demographic transition to ever increasing numbers of older people, and the costs of old age. The governments of the world have largely chosen to exert a great deal of control over the development and provision of medicine, to the point of it becoming an expense for them, a burden much akin to the mess that was made of pension entitlements, the creation of large enough promises of future expenditure to financially ruin the systems created to manage them. Treatments for aging are a deus ex machina that will save the system, or that is the hope being pushed into government circles by advocates attempting to achieve greater support for the development of longevity therapeutics. The realpolitik always seems somewhat shabby in full daylight when it departs utterly from the considerations of what aging does to an individual, physically and mentally. The true reason to build therapies to treat aging is because this offers the strong possibility of a very sizable reduction in human suffering and death, not because it can prop up dysfunction systems of governance.
The longevity dividend: Why governments and markets must catch up

'How much' often matters less than 'how fast'. Financial systems might comfortably accommodate a decade increase in life expectancy if it emerges gradually over half a century, but could they accommodate the same increase within 5 years? Economies are built to absorb gradual change and are much less comfortable with discontinuities. Human longevity may be approaching that kind of discontinuity . The latest scientific advances point to the emergence of what we have termed 'system-level' therapeutics capable of bringing about rapid, non-linear changes in both healthspan and lifespan trajectories, challenging the incremental paradigms that underpin current economic and demographic forecasting models. If they do, governments, healthcare systems, insurers and pension funds will have to respond to a break with history, not a continuation of it.

Public debate often treats longevity as a cost curve. That is only half the ledger. In an era of demographic ageing and stagnant economic growth forecasts, one overlooked truth is emerging: longevity science may be the most powerful economic productivity lever of all time. Governments spend billions annually on education, digital transformation and industrial innovation - all in the name of boosting national productivity. Yet few acknowledge that the single largest drag on workforce participation is declining health in midlife and beyond due to ageing. In the United States, the direct costs of chronic health conditions total around $1.1 trillion - equivalent to 5.8% of US gross domestic product (GDP). When indirect costs of lost economic productivity are included, the total costs of chronic diseases in the United States increase to $3.7 trillion - in other words, they equate to almost 20% of the US GDP.

The economic argument for longevity research is clear: targeting the root causes of ageing is not just a healthcare imperative, it is set to become a non-negotiable economic strategy. Governments should treat it as such, allocating funding accordingly and incentivising translational research , clinical trials, and public-private partnerships in this field. In the 20th century, public investment in antibiotics and vaccines changed the world. In the 21st century, ageing biology has the potential to do the same.

bodyOriginal.text: Inspired by shapes and movement found in nature, Pablo Luna Studio conceives of hospitality spaces, wellness retreats, and homes that sympathize with their surroundings. Rather than creating a barrier between outside and inside, the airy structures welcome foliage and the natural landscape into the overall experience, blurring the boundary between structure and environment.

The firm, based in Ubud, Bali, Indonesia, is dedicated to building with nature, incorporating sustainable materials and taking a climate-responsive approach. “Imagine a home that stays cool in summer without constant air conditioning, or warm in winter with minimal heating, simply by virtue of its design,” the studio says. “This isn’t magic; it’s the intelligent application of climate responsive architecture. It’s about leveraging natural forces like sun, wind, and rain, transforming them from challenges into design opportunities.”

bodyOriginal.alt: an interior view of wooden architecture in an undulating, organic form

bodyOriginal.text: Recent projects include the Lotus Shala in Ubud, which takes the lotus—a symbol of purity and awakening—as inspiration for an elegantly concave wooden canopy with open sides supported by posts, so that those inside feel connected to their tropical surroundings. It’s built entirely from bamboo, which is an incredibly strong yet flexible material, allowing the team to create graceful curves complemented by geometric precision.

In Sanskrit, “shala” means “home,” and the spiritual practice of yoga is complemented by purpose-built pavilion designs that encourage harmony and calm. Pablo Luna Studio’s Manta Shala is yet another example, perched on the coastline of Nusa Penida, Indonesia, with an undulating roofline that evokes the way a manta ray’s body creates a gentle, wave-like motion as it swims.
Additional projects include an eco-lodge in Uganda and numerous villas, restaurants, and wellness destinations in Bali. See more on the studio’s Instagram .

bodyOriginal.text: Sarcopenia is the name given to severe age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. This loss occurs steadily throughout later life. The present state of research into this condition is representative of aging more generally, in that while a range of quite different mechanisms all have strong supporting evidence for a meaningful contribution to sarcopenia, their relative importance to one another is unclear, how they connect to one another at the detail level is unclear, which are largely causes and which are largely consequences of one another, and their relationship to the known underlying forms of cell and tissue damage that drive aging is unclear. See the evidence for loss of muscle stem cell function to be the primary cause of sarcopenia, and surrounding discussions on that topic, for example. Here, researchers point instead to disruption of lactate metabolism in both liver and muscle tissue as the primary cause of sarcopenia; the involvement of the liver a reminder that no one tissue stands alone in the matter of aging. All organs communicate with one another and are interdependent in many different ways.

Sarcopenia is a progressive disease characterized by age-related decline in skeletal muscle force and mass. The fundamental molecular pathogenesis of sarcopenia has not yet been elucidated. Here, we show that the accumulation of lactate and intracellular acidification, lactic acidosis , in skeletal muscle owing to impaired liver-skeletal muscle lactate metabolism is the fundamental cause of sarcopenia. Systemic lactate tolerance decreased in aged mice owing to the impaired lactate processing capacity in the liver, which caused lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle.

Furthermore, pharmacological activation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) or liver-specific activation of HIF1α improved age-associated impairment in lactate tolerance, lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle, and sarcopenia. Mechanistically, the decreased nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide level was the cause of dysregulated skeletal muscle functions due to lactic acidosis. Using mouse models , our results show lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle as a key molecular pathogenesis of sarcopenia and highlight HIF1α in the liver as a pharmacological target for sarcopenia.

bodyOriginal.text: Normal cell metabolism , particularly the activities of mitochondria , generates oxidizing molecules that react with proteins to disrupt their function. This damage occurs constantly, and is repaired constantly. Cells remove damaged proteins, undo oxidative changes, and make use of antioxidant enzymes such as SOD1 to prevent damage from occurring in the first place. With age, oxidation increases and becomes an important component of cell dysfunction. Here, researchers note that SOD1 itself can become oxidized and harmful, and discuss the importance of antioxidants disabled by oxidization in the growth of age-related oxidative stress in cells. The specific focus is on skin aging, but the points have relevance to all tissues.

As the body's primary barrier against environmental insults, the skin is continually exposed to oxidative stress, which may contribute to progressive proteotoxic stress. Excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) can overwhelm cellular protein-quality-control systems, promoting the accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins, proteome instability, and eventual protein homeostasis ( proteostasis ) collapse. Superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) , a Cu/Zn-dependent cytosolic antioxidant enzyme and key component of cellular defense against superoxide radicals, is itself vulnerable to oxidative modification. ROS-mediated post-translational oxidation of SOD1 may promote its misfolding and the formation of toxic protein species, potentially establishing a self-amplifying cycle of superoxide accumulation, further protein damage, and impaired cellular homeostasis .

In cutaneous cell types, including dermal fibroblasts and epidermal cells, these processes may be especially relevant to age-associated declines in proteostatic capacity and skin aging. This review distinguishes established skin-specific evidence from hypotheses extrapolated from other systems and synthesizes current evidence on the interplay among ROS-induced protein damage, proteostasis failure, SOD1 dysfunction, and cutaneous aging. We highlight the bidirectional relationship between proteostasis collapse and mitochondrial dysfunction , which may establish a self-reinforcing cycle of oxidative stress, cellular senescence , and chronic low-grade inflammation . These interconnected processes may converge to promote extracellular-matrix remodeling and tissue dysfunction, contributing to wrinkles, reduced elasticity, and impaired barrier function.

articles.summaryOriginal: Craft has become cool, while industrial design has lost its sparkle. What's driving the trend? And are they really so different? Debika Ray reports. 'Handmade', 'heritage', 'bespoke' – most of us are used to reading these words by now. Just like the food industry before it, the world of design has internalised the language of The post How craft conquered design appeared first on Dezeen .

bodyOriginal.text: Craft has become cool, while industrial design has lost its sparkle. What's driving the trend? And are they really so different? Debika Ray reports.

'Handmade', 'heritage', 'bespoke' – most of us are used to reading these words by now. Just like the food industry before it, the world of design has internalised the language of craft – that of the 'local', 'artisanal' and 'authentic'.
At London Design Festival (LDF) this year, exhibitions of craft abound.

These range from Reviving Craft at Somerset House , a show of more than 60 artisans from China curated by Beijing-based media entrepreneur Yang Lan to "create a dialogue between traditional craftsmanship and contemporary design", to Wood for the Trees at the Tab Centre in Shoreditch , an "abstracted woodland" in which to contemplate responsible forestry, designed by London-based Mitre & Mondays for the American Hardwood Export Council .

bodyOriginal.alt: Symbiosis of Chrysanthemums II by Huang Lu

bodyOriginal.text: Among many craft-based exhibitions at this year's LDF is Reviving Craft, featuring pieces such as Symphony of Chrysanthemums II by Huang Lu. Photo courtesy of Reviving Craft From Milan to Copenhagen, it's the same story: where once objects on display were proudly modernist, minimalist, sleek and uniform, they are now just as likely to be textured and imperfect.
The growing status of collectible design is part of the same movement – the desire for unique objects met by the inherent unpredictability of the human hand.
Pavel Klimczak, founder of design retailer Monologue London , has noticed this desire in the questions his customers now ask him.

"People are becoming much more curious about the stories behind objects," he said. "They often come for the design, but quickly the conversation turns to them asking where a piece was made, who made it, how it was made, why it was designed that way and the material used."

Craft was once dowdy. Now it's cool. And industrial design – that 20th-century emblem of democratised mass production, functional innovation and accessible beauty – has, whether fairly or unfairly, somewhat lost its sheen.
What underlying social and economic tensions does this shift reveal? And, beyond face value, is the line between 'craft' and 'design' especially meaningful in the first place?

The growing interest in craft is often attributed to our modern condition: the frictionless and ephemeral nature of our daily interactions, the cold dead pieces of technology we're continuously pawing, the deceptive nature of digital content, and the stylistic uniformity imposed over decades by globalised mass production and online connectivity.
In that context, it's no surprise we're drawn to unique objects that carry traces of human intention, are made of materials we recognise and are connected to a time, person and place.

A greater interest in the local, in heritage and in the vernacular also tracks with the current political mood: the simultaneous return, globally, of traditional values and a growing focus on cultures that have long been marginalised by modernisation and globalisation.
London Craft Week founder Guy Salter is convinced that our renewed interest in craft is here to stay.

"It's not going anywhere soon, as it's built on solid foundations – on more than just fashionability," he said. "We're rediscovering [things about quality of workmanship] that our forefathers knew for hundreds of years."
"And whenever I travel, I meet people who aren't attracted by the glossiness of luxury brands, but instead feel pleased to be supporting craft on a community basis."

bodyOriginal.alt: Bamboo baskets with hand-blown glass made by Dima Srouji for a Gucci exhibition at Milan design week 2025

bodyOriginal.text: Gucci is among the brands to have incorporated craft into its presence at design festivals, as with these baskets made by Dima Srouji for an exhibition at Milan design week 2025. Photo by George Baggaley Drawing on this interest, London Craft Week (pictured top) now attracts about 250,000 visitors every year – up from about 35,000 a decade ago – which compares robustly to LDF's 475,000 in 2025.

This year, in a boost for its credentials, fashion designer Jonathan Anderson – who set up the €50,000 Loewe Craft Prize while creative director of the Spanish luxury house – came on board as a sponsor via his own brand, JW Anderson .
Alberto Merlo Carrero, Loewe Foundation's head of programmes, says the founding of the prize in 2016 was a recognition that contemporary craft was on the ascent.
"Extraordinary work was already happening around the world, yet the field remained relatively fragmented and often underrepresented within the broader cultural conversation," he said.
Fashion brands from Hermès to Gucci now more often than not tend to showcase craft in their increasingly visible presence at design weeks.
Fostering a healthy craft ecosystem requires long-term commitment, which – more broadly – hasn't always been evident.

Salter says the expansion and corporatisation of the luxury sector in recent years has shaken up a business model that a century ago was mostly based on "a small number of customers buying or commissioning from what were often family-owned luxury shops".

In the process of trying to attract a mass audience, he explains, money was channelled into marketing via flagship stores and advertising, with craft often taking a hit – the in-house artisan replaced by outsourced production, for example.
"Now, a number of brands have realised what was lost during that period, especially during the recent downturn, and are trying to retrofit it," he said.
Against that backdrop, Salter says, craft has become a marker of quality and trustworthiness.

He adds that, while initially those new "aspirational customers" they were after took brands at their word, today's buyers are more discerning, and trust companies with a track record of standing by their values.

bodyOriginal.alt: Peaches chair by Lara Bohinc

bodyOriginal.text: Lara Bohinc has worked in industrial design as well as making objects by hand, including the Peaches chair. Photo by Rebecca Reid In contrast, industrial design is facing a "difficult predicament" as people increasingly question the ethics and purpose of mass production, according to London-based designer Lara Bohinc , who has collaborated with brands for decades and recently started working with clay.
"We're drowning in products. There are too many brands, too many chairs, too many beds," she said.

Meanwhile, cheaper design is often associated with bad labour practices, unsustainable processes or toxic materials – factors that are often ignored because these products are what most people can afford.
Calling something craft and charging a lot for it doesn't necessarily change the ethics behind an object, though.

Between 2023 and 2026, luxury fashion brands including Armani, Dior and Valentino were placed under court monitoring in Italy after investigations found they had outsourced production to illegal workshops where undocumented migrants were working under exploitative conditions on supposedly artisanal products.
"Just because it's handmade doesn't mean it's angelic," Bohinc points out.
"Few are making money exclusively from selling objects they've made"

Andu Masebo , a London designer who creates functional objects and art pieces in wood and metal, says he never had a "romantic notion" around craft – rather, he started making his designs simply because of the difficulty of finding a company willing to produce them for him.
He points out that the rise of craft isn't only a story about what consumers want, but also of what the industry is producing.

For designers, for example, the move to making is often driven by a fragile job market in which brands favour existing names over investing in new work, leaving emerging designers with few options but to produce things themselves.

"I feel like there could be a more positive conversation around how we create conditions that allow people to work in design and not just in the gallery space, and a concerted effort by the industry to reach out to emerging talent, not just as a marketing tool but as a way of supporting the future design pool," he said.
While craft may be in vogue, Masebo has observed that making itself doesn't necessarily offer a more sustainable livelihood than working for a design company.
"Few of my peers are making money exclusively from selling objects and furniture they've made," he said.

bodyOriginal.alt: A4 lamp by Andu Masebo

bodyOriginal.text: Andu Masebo says he started making his own pieces, such as the A4 lamp, because of a lack of alternatives. Photo courtesy of Unit.d Instead, they use it to "express the highest version of their practice", while generating an income for themselves by diffusing that into a range of other related and unrelated sources, from social media to part-time jobs to commissions.

As Bohinc and Masebo highlight, categories such as craft and design may be useful from a marketing perspective, but underlying both are similar dynamics and challenges about quality, labour, employment and environmental impact that the sector cannot escape simply by changing how it describes work.
These extractive practices are among the subjects Nigerian-American designer Zoë Chinonso Ene is striving to address through her research and experiment-driven studio Homenkà .

In reality, she argues, craft and design aren't mutually exclusive categories, and the way we use those terms reveals underlying hierarchies in the value we place on different cultures of production – often based on aesthetic cues such as particular motifs, materials and styles.

"For example, with everyday objects from Igbo culture, I can see the decisions that were made to create object typologies for specific uses," said Ene, questioning why these are called craft rather than design.

Read: How London designers are making it work For LDF, Homenkà is creating an intervention as part of Brompton Design District – a parlour that will host evenings of play, eating, conversation and remembering "in the company of everyday design".
Its broader focus is on supporting craft ecosystems in Nigeria. In envisioning these, Ene isn't a purist about the separation between hand and machine.

"It may mean artisans working in a semi-industrialised space where they do 50 per cent, not 100 per cent, by hand, to speed it up while creating a fantastic product whose materials are sourced locally and gaining and exchanging skills," she said.
London designer Bethan Laura Wood has always straddled both worlds. She recalls that during her student days "craft was a dirty word in relation to design" – certainly not the case today.

For LDF, she is showing work as part of Craft x Tech , an exhibition by design studio Tangent that brings artisans from the Tōkai region of Japan together with international designers – in her case, to create folded hanging lamps made with shibori tie-dyeing company Suzusan .
Wood points out that public interest is like a pendulum – shifting from minimalism to maximalism, machine production to craft making – even as all these things continue to exist all at once.

bodyOriginal.alt: Nchọ by Homenkà, showing at LDF 2026

bodyOriginal.text: Zoë Chinonso Ene's designs drawing on Igbo culture at showing at this year's LDF. Photo by Christian Cassiel The reactionary resurgence of craft is also not a new thing – think of the Arts and Crafts movement emerging in response to the industrial revolution, she adds.
That's not to dismiss the significance of what's happening now: waves of fashion can leave behind more substantive and meaningful change.

"When industry started to pay more attention to recyclability or circular design , some companies just flirted with those ideas to tick boxes, but others adopted it into their systems in a long-term way," said Wood.
Similarly, beautifully produced videos revealing the process behind objects – the metal spinning, the turning pots, the scraping of lathes – probably won't dominate social media algorithms forever.

articles.titleOriginal: Are you getting ghosted more than ever? You're not alone!
articles.summaryOriginal: It's not about you; it's about a broken business culture. You've spent a lot of time, effort and emotional energy forging a working relationship. It's all going well. Then… nothing. The founder who sa...

bodyOriginal.text: It's not about you; it's about a broken business culture.

You've spent a lot of time, effort and emotional energy forging a working relationship. It's all going well. Then… nothing. The founder who said they loved your first concept simply vanishes. A marketing lead who's briefed you thoroughly and has promised a purchase order suddenly leaves you high and dry.

It's a horrible situation to be in. From a financial standpoint alone, it can be crippling. But more fundamentally, you also start to doubt yourself. Was the quote too high? Were the concepts lame? Did they find someone cheaper, or use AI? Did you have some food on your face during the Zoom call that everyone was too polite to point out?

Horrific, right? But here's what we've learned from our community on LinkedIn and Instagram . In 2026, ghosting has become systemic. So you shouldn't take it personally. Because it's not really about you at all.

Why silence has become the default "I've seen a lot of this so far this year, and it can feel really hollow at times," says director and cinematographer Rob Pinney . "I'm still getting a good number of approaches for new projects, but many more of those now end up with a dead email chain than before."

So what's behind the trend? "There seems to be a lot more budget hesitancy right now," Rob suggests. "And I suspect some of that is to do with clients weighing up that potential spend on video production, in my case, versus what they could do with it elsewhere, including with AI tools."

Film director Farai Dube has had similar experiences. "It's a lot of stop and start," he says. "When you're at the start of the conversation, there's actually a budget, but that's in jeopardy depending on sales and generally how much money's coming in. I get that: the part that's frustrating is keeping you on the hook. I'd rather have clarity upfront."

Yet it's not just cash-strapped clients who are guilty of ghosting. Creative director Rich Holt , for instance, complains about "recruiters who appeal for specific people to contact them—even though they're supposed to know the industry and have CVs on their desk already—and then just never reply." Director and lecturer Luke Tonge , meanwhile, calls out: "folks not replying when you invite them to speak at an event. It can hold up planning for weeks and even months."
So why does ghosting seem to be getting so much worse these days?

The fear factor Graphic designer and photo retoucher Sandrine Bascouert reckons there's something deeper going on than just laziness or poor organisation. "I think some people are afraid of communication as a whole," she says. "Ghosting has become a way to avoid normal conversations where there could be feelings hurt and disappointment."

That certainly chimes with my experience as a member of Generation X. When I first entered journalism in the 1990s, almost the entire job was phoning people. As long as you were polite and respectful, everyone was happy to chat.

By around the mid-2000s, though, I noticed that many creatives under 30 were screening their calls and wouldn't pick up if they didn't know the caller personally, even if they were actively trying to promote themselves and their work, which never made any sense to me.

Eventually I admitted defeat, and switched to email. But by the mid-2010s, many creatives were keeping their emails private—despite, again, ostensibly wanting self-promotion—and I had to start relying on social media DMs instead.

In 2026, many of those creatives are now seniors and CEOs. So it's no surprise to me that some might lack the ability to have difficult conversations, and not be willing to put in the emotional labour when times get difficult. I don't wish to generalise about an entire generation, of course. But still.

Good reason or bad actor? Poor communication skills, though, are only one reason for ghosting: there are plenty more. If we're being generous, for instance, we might assume that there's been something like a family emergency, and the other party just doesn't have the capacity to even open their inbox right now.

At the other end of the spectrum, some people can just be dicks. We've all heard of companies who interview people, ask for their ideas, and then simply steal them. There was never any job, freelance work or collaboration opportunity in the first place. It was all a scam.

Then there are those who sit somewhere in the middle, who aren't malicious, but just fail to cope. That doesn't help you , of course. As designer Nicholas Robb points out: "It starts to feel unfair after you've done a couple of calls with the stakeholders, bordering on consultation to help them scope it up. It would take 30 seconds to email back and say 'not interested + a reason why'."

Yet as an entrepreneur himself, he can also empathise. "I think business owners in particular are just so overwhelmed these days that they can't afford the time or mental space to do even that," he reflects. "So I try not to take it personally."
How we should respond Other than not beating yourself up for being ghosted, though, what can you practically do?

As a rule of thumb, designer Alexander Clark has developed a script. "After two or three of my emails go unreplied, I write this", he says, " Since I've not heard from you, I'll be pausing this and moving forward with other projects. Please let me know when you'd like to proceed or if you've changed priorities. " It usually yields a response within a day."

This is a good strategy because it removes all ambiguity. You've stopped chasing them (giving them the power) and are about to close the door (giving you the power). They have no choice but to make a decision. At this point, silence and doing nothing becomes a decision in itself.

And if that's what happens? Then move on, feeling empowered that you took control of the situation. And remember: their silence is not a poor reflection on you; it's a poor reflection on their lack of professionalism and communication skills.

Setting boundaries upfront Ultimately, prevention is always better than cure. So if you want to avoid getting ghosted, it's always good to set boundaries upfront, such as a deadline for responding to proposals. That might seem a little overbearing, but remember that clients and employers are often super-busy, and a deadline can actually be helpful for them too.

Content creator Jacob Elias Nurse offers a further suggestion: have a lot of plates spinning. "One thing I've learned from my nine months of being a full-time freelancer is that keeping busy helps you not worry too much about replies from companies that want to dangle a carrot in your face," he explains. "If you keep grinding at your craft, the money will follow."

He even finds a way to frame ghosting as a positive . As he puts it: "Their disrespect isn't a reflection of your craft or your quote. If anything, it helps you weed out who you want as a client and who you don't want as one."

Founder and creative director Kirsten Murray agrees. "A person who ghosts you is not someone you want to work with," she says. "Mutual respect and open communication make for the best creative partnerships."

So maybe that's the main takeaway. Ghosting sucks, for sure, but it's not necessarily a calamity. In fact, in the long term, it could be a good thing: saving you from a nightmare client and freeing you up to find a good'un instead.

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion : Trimble SketchUp will bring its 3D Basecamp Summit to Las Vegas , exploring how artificial intelligence (AI) and reality capture are changing the way projects are designed, visualised and built.

Taking place from 9 to 11 November at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas, the 3D Basecamp Summit will form part of Trimble Dimensions , a conference bringing together users of Trimble 's technology across architecture, engineering and construction.

The three-day event will focus on the increasingly connected workflow between a designer's digital toolkit and the physical building site, combining hands-on workshops, technical sessions and talks from designers and industry experts.

bodyOriginal.alt: An attendee looking at presentation boards showing student projects

bodyOriginal.text: The 3D Basecamp Summit takes place at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas One of the biggest themes will be the use of AI as a design tool, with sessions exploring how generative AI can automate repetitive modelling tasks while allowing designers to retain control over their work.
The programme will also look at how sketches and images can be converted into editable 3D geometry and how natural-language prompts can be used to generate models and tools.

bodyOriginal.alt: An attendee uses a stylus to navigate a detailed 3D interior model displayed on a tablet

bodyOriginal.text: The summit will include workshops, technical sessions and talks The summit will examine how existing buildings can be brought into digital design workflows through reality capture such as scan-to-BIM, a process that uses scanning technology such as LiDAR to capture an existing physical environment and turn it into a digital model. This information can then be used alongside architectural models, connecting measurements taken on site with work being developed in the studio.
The summit will demonstrate how these models can move between the building site and design studio, rather than leaving information locked in separate silos.
The programme also covers interoperability between design, engineering and fabrication software, alongside extensions and coding that allow practices to customise their workflows.

bodyOriginal.alt: Three attendees talking in a lounge area at the 3D Basecamp Summit

bodyOriginal.text: The summit brings together SketchUp users, designers and industry experts Among the speakers is London-based interior designer Tola Ojuolape , who will discuss how she uses SketchUp to translate digital interiors into physical, material-led installations.
Ojuolape previously collaborated with Dezeen and SketchUp on a Design Workshop, using the software to develop a fictional three-storey library in London's Clerkenwell.
Other speakers include Jason Li of global workplace design practice M Moser and urban planner Devin Lavigne of Houseal Lavigne .

The summit will also include a panel moderated by Dezeen co-CEO Benedict Hobson, bringing together Ojuolape, M Moser and Programa to discuss the use of digital tools in commercial interiors and retail design.

bodyOriginal.alt: An attendee pointing to a laptop screen showing a SketchUp model

bodyOriginal.text: Participants will take part in hands-on SketchUp modelling workshops The event will also feature the SketchUp Ascent Competition, where students and educators will present their 3D modelling projects live, with finalists pitching their work to an audience at Trimble Dimensions.

SketchUp is a 3D modelling platform used across architecture, interior design, engineering and construction. Trimble, which acquired SketchUp in 2012, develops software and hardware used across the built environment, including technologies for surveying, design, construction and asset management.
The 2026 3D Basecamp Summit takes place from 9 to 11 November at The Venetian Resort in Las Vegas and registration is now open .

bodyOriginal.text: Design student Gargi Agrawalla has won this year's UK James Dyson Award with a device that uses artificial intelligence to alert deaf and hard-of-hearing users of important sounds like knocks or fire alarms, which they might otherwise miss.
More than 500 samples were used to train the SIVO.GO system so it can recognise these noises and translate them into vibrations and flashing lights, rousing the user without the need for sound.

bodyOriginal.alt: Person in bed reaching for an alarm

bodyOriginal.text: Gargi Agrawalla has designed an AI-powered alarm for deaf and hard-of-hearing people To design the alarm, the Loughborough University graduate drew on her own experience of being born profoundly deaf before receiving a cochlear implant at age 12. Although the implant allowed her to hear sounds for the first time, she discovered that its external sound processor had to be removed when sleeping or showering, which left her feeling uneasy in foreign environments.
"SIVO.GO came from my own experience as a deaf cochlear implant user and the anxiety I felt when travelling or staying somewhere unfamiliar," Agrawalla told Dezeen.

bodyOriginal.alt: SIVO.GO alarm for deaf users by Gargi Agrawalla, winner of 2026 UK James Dyson Award

bodyOriginal.text: SIVO.GO runs on an algorithm trained on more than 500 noise samples Existing alarms for the hard-of-hearing tend to be bulky and expensive, the student found.
Often, they are also geared towards only one particular sound like fire alarms or a crying baby, requiring users to pack a whole arsenal of gadgets when travelling.

bodyOriginal.alt: Alarms used by deaf and hard-of-hearing people

bodyOriginal.text: It was designed to replace existing clunky, single-purpose devices "As a cochlear implant user, I already have to think about equipment such as chargers, a dry box and waterproof accessories, so adding several more safety devices creates extra stress," Agrawalla said.
"I wanted to reduce that burden by creating one portable system that could cover several important alerts and give deaf and hard-of-hearing users more reassurance when away from home."

Read: Urify is a toilet-cleaning tablet that helps diagnose kidney disease To achieve this, SIVO.GO uses an AI model trained on more than 500 sound samples, allowing it to distinguish between a range of different noises, from door bells to alarms.
This model is run locally on the device, rather than through Wi-Fi or the cloud, preserving user's privacy while ensuring reliability even in the absence of an internet connection.
To detect knocking or forced entry, the sound processor is also supported by a separate vibration sensor that can be attached to a door.

bodyOriginal.alt: Vibration sensor or SIVO.GO alarm for deaf users

bodyOriginal.text: The AI is supported by a vibration sensor "During testing, door knocking caused too many false positives because the AI could confuse it with similar sounds such as footsteps or tapping on a table, even after adding more training samples," Agrawalla said.

articles.titleOriginal: An Entirely New Target for Fighting Senescence
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence. Very little previous work In […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence .

Very little previous work In most papers, after a customary discussion of the mechanics of cellular senescence and current methods of handling it and its repercussions, the researchers go on to discuss previous work relating to the particular approach at hand. However, that does not pertain to this paper; PTCHD4 is only known as being structurally related to PTCH1, which affects the Hedgehog signaling pathway [1]. While some work has linked dysregulation of Hedgehog pathways to accelerated neurodegeneration [2], the specific role of PTCHD4 was not clear.

The researchers found that, when exposed to the genotoxin bleomycin, PTCHD4 increases alongside inflammation markers in a variety of cells, including human fetal lung diploid fibroblasts, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), alveolar epithelial type II cells (AEC2s), human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and adult retinal pigment epithelial cells. Aging Atlas data confirmed this upregulation in other types of cells as well, and NCBI data listed this molecule as being disease-associated: its presence is negligible under ordinary conditions.

The team then examined young mice, old mice, and progeric mice, staining for PTCHD4 alongside the senescence biomarker p16. The two biomarkers were expressed in similar quantities among each group in multiple tissues. Similar results were found in human tissue samples; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) patients expressed more PTCHD4 in their lungs than people without the disease, and human lung cells expressing PTCHD4 were more likely to also express established senescence markers.

Significant effects on senescence The next experiment involved creating MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 and then driving them senescent through replication. PTCHD4 was found to be a critical driver of senescence in this group; after an average of eight passages, ordinary MEFs exhibited signs of senescence, such as the key biomarker SA-β-gal, while this did not occur to the PTCHD4-deficient MEFs until an average of passage 14.

This line of experimentation continued with PTCHD4-overexpressing MEFs, which began exhibiting senescence-related features such as SA-β-gal early in passage 5. Similar results were found in AEC2s; the inflammatory biomarkers IL6 and IL8, along with SA-β-gal, were upregulated alongside PTCHD4 overexpression.

This testing continued with live mice. The researchers utilized mice that do not express PTCHD4 along with wild-type mice, and they exposed both groups to D-galactose, which mimics many of the symptoms of natural aging. The mice that did not express PTCHD4 were much more resistant to D-galactose than wild-type mice, and there were no detectable physical or biochemical problems caused by this absence.

The team then continued with naturally aging animals. They found that mice that do not express PTCHD4 naturally live months longer than wild-type mice, and mice without it apparenly do not develop white hair the way that wild-type animals do.

bodyOriginal.alt: PTCHD4 aging

bodyOriginal.text: A further experiment involved subjecting mice to bleomycin, which harms lung function in a way that mimics IPF in people. As expected, the mice exhibited features of lung fibrosis within 21 days. However, the PTCHD4-less mice suffered from fewer symptoms of the disease, retaining more lung capacity, less immune infiltration, less destruction of alveolar tissues, and less fibrosis than wild-type mice.

A well-known signaling pathway In this study, PTCHD4 was found to have no effects on the Hedgehog pathway or related genes. Instead, its effects were found to be due to AKT signaling. AKT activation normally increases with aging, but a lack of PTCHD4 diminished this. The team created MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 but express AKT through a different construct, and these MEFs were not protected by their lack of PTCHD4. Similar experiments involving the direct expression of AKT in other cell types confirmed these results, recapitulating the effects of PTCHD4.

The researchers believe that “PTCHD4 may represent a candidate target for senescence-associated interventions” and that there is “a potential role for PTCHD4 in age-related fibrotic disease.” However, this is an initial study. Further work will need to be done to confirm these results, elucidate the relationship of PTCHD4 and AKT, ascertain any side effects of eliminating or suppressing PTCHD4, and determine if PTCHD4 can be targeted by interventions.

bodyOriginal.text: A few species of hydra are immortal in their normal environmental conditions, meaning that function does not decline over time and mortality risk does not increase over time. Researchers spent a good deal of time taking care of hundreds of hydra some years ago to demonstrate that this is the case . Hydra are lower animals, essentially a bundle of stem cells capable of regenerating and replacing any part of their bodies, somewhat analogous to an ambulatory embryo. It is an open question as to whether anything we can learn from their biochemistry can be useful in human medicine.

In today's open access paper, researchers report on the employment of telomerase by hydra. Telomeres are repeated sequences at the end of chromosomes that shorten with each cell replication , creating a clock that leads to cell death when telomeres are too short. In most species, somatic cells are limited in this way in order to minimize the risk of cancer, while stem cells employ telomerase to maintain long telomeres while delivering a supply of new daughter somatic cells to replace losses. The body is just a temporary vehicle for an immortal population of germline stem cells, in one view. Hydra are obvious very different in terms of the balance between stem cell behavior versus somatic cell behavior in individuals.
Telomerase expression and activity in the immortal cnidarian Hydra

Most living eumetazoan animals are mortal. A fundamental mechanism underlying cellular and organismal aging in many species is the progressive shortening of telomeres - protective nucleoprotein structures at chromosome ends. The finite replicative lifespan of somatic cells is linked to telomere attrition. The discovery of telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein complex with reverse transcriptase activity that synthesizes telomeric repeats, provided a molecular explanation for the unlimited proliferative potential of germlines, stem cells, and most cancer cells. In humans, telomerase is not expressed in most somatic tissues and is active primarily in germ cells, stem cells, and certain rapidly renewing tissues such as blood or intestinal epithelium .

Comparative studies indicate that telomere dynamics correlate with lifespan, with slower shortening rates in long-lived species. Recent cross-species analyses, however, reveal a more complex picture, suggesting that the relationship between telomere maintenance strategies (telomerase activity vs. alternative lengthening ) and longevity is not strictly deterministic. Nevertheless, it remains a prevailing hypothesis that biologically immortal organisms must possess robust mechanisms for telomere maintenance. Supporting this, sustained telomerase activity in somatic tissues has been documented in non-senescent invertebrate models such as planarians and long-lived bivalves .

Importantly, several taxa , including some hydras, planarians, and rotifers , have been reported to exhibit negligible or undetectable senescence. In this study, we characterized the telomerase of Hydra vulgaris . The expression pattern of the telomerase catalytic subunit (hyTERT) mRNA correlates with regions exhibiting high proliferative potential and remains unchanged during budding or regeneration. These findings were further corroborated by measurements of telomerase activity. Our data suggest that telomerase may play a role in the immortality of Hydra.

articles.titleOriginal: Asymptomatic Persistent Infection as a Contribution to Degenerative Aging
articles.summaryOriginal: Persistent infections such as cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses most likely accelerate aging, primarily via harmful effects on the immune system that lead to earlier immunosenescence and chronic inflammation than would otherwise be the case. A range of mechanistic and epidemiological research broadly supports this hypothesis. It remains challenging to completely clear persistent viral infect

bodyOriginal.text: Persistent infections such as cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses most likely accelerate aging, primarily via harmful effects on the immune system that lead to earlier immunosenescence and chronic inflammation than would otherwise be the case. A range of mechanistic and epidemiological research broadly supports this hypothesis. It remains challenging to completely clear persistent viral infections, however. If a strong antiviral therapy existed , epidemiological data would likely prove the point one way or another within five to ten years, as effects on aging would become apparent in older populations. As it stands, the present relatively weak antiviral therapies show some evidence for positive effects on late life risk of mortality and age-related disease, but not in all studies.

Asymptomatic infections are traditionally considered harmless, reflecting effective immune control and the absence of clinical disease. Yet growing evidence shows that these silent encounters with microbes are far from being immunologically neutral. Throughout life, humans are challenged by a remarkably broad spectrum of viruses and bacteria, including latent pathogens that persist, fluctuate, or periodically reactivate without producing significant symptoms. From an evolutionary standpoint, this represents a fundamental trade-off. Long-lived hosts benefit from maintaining diverse commensal , latent, and low-grade persistent microbes that enhance immune readiness, promote cross-protective immunity , and reduce vulnerability to severe infections. However, this adaptive advantage is counterbalanced by the continuous burden of chronic, almost undetectable immune activation and inflammation, and by the energetic cost of sustaining such mechanisms of surveillance.

In this regard, retroviral integrations provide a striking illustration of how persistent viral presence has shaped the evolution of complex organisms by introducing new regulatory elements , immune modulators, and developmental programs. These ancient viral imprints demonstrate that clinically-silent host-microbe interactions can exert long-term selective pressures and influence species-specific biological trajectories. At the individual level, repeated asymptomatic infections trigger transient waves of immune activation, endothelial perturbation, mitochondrial stress, and complement engagement. Although each episode is mild and self-limited, their cumulative burden generates micro-damage that accelerates immunosenescence, perturbs metabolic and vascular homeostasis , and contributes to the progressive rise in systemic inflammation characteristic of aging.

articles.summaryOriginal: Cells become senescent constantly throughout life in response to various forms of damage and stress, ceasing replication and generating a potent mix of inflammatory signals. bodyOriginal.text: Cells become senescent constantly throughout life in response to various forms of damage and stress, ceasing replication and generating a potent mix of inflammatory signals. In youth, these cells are promptly cleared by the immune system , but with advancing age they begin to linger and accumulate. The inflammatory signaling becomes disruptive to tissue structure and function when sustained over the long term, and this is an important contribution to degenerative aging. Here, researchers show that macrophage cells in the kidney express increasing amounts of the P2RX7 receptor on the cell surface as they progress towards becoming senescent, and blocking this receptor with a suitable antagonist small molecule reduces macrophage senescence and improves kidney function.

Macrophage senescence is a pathological feature in aging or diseased kidneys. However, the role of senescent macrophages in kidney injury and aging has not been fully elucidated yet. We integrated the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing datasets and the adoptively transfusion of pretreated bone marrow-derived macrophages to investigate the role of renal macrophage senescence in kidney injury. Here, we portrayed the senescence trajectory along multiple time points in infiltrating macrophages, and observed the persistent increase of macrophage-expressed purinergic receptor P2RX7 along the senescence trajectory in injured kidneys of septic mice.

Importantly, our discovered small-molecule P2RX7 antagonist strikingly improved kidney function and pathological damage, as well as mitigated macrophage senescence in septic and aging mice. Mechanistically, P2RX7 antagonist could promote the wound healing , migration , and proliferation capacity of senescent reparative macrophages, thus exerting anti-inflammatory effects and repairing kidney tissues. Together, our findings illustrate the crucial participation of senescent macrophages in septic kidney injury, and offer novel therapeutic strategy via intervening P2RX7 against immunosenescence -associated kidney injury and aging.
